justice: Street space is heavily allocated to motor vehicles (multiple travel lanes and extensive curbside parking), while pedestrian space appears narrow behind metal railings, indicating an unequal distribution of public right-of-way for non-drivers.

Large amounts of curb space are occupied by parked cars and clusters of parked scooters/motorbikes near storefronts, which can limit access to the commercial frontage for different users (people walking, deliveries, families).

Accessibility is only moderate because the pedestrian path is visually constrained by continuous guardrails and storefront spillover (parked scooters), and no clear curb ramps/tactile guidance are visible from this viewpoint.
safety: Guardrails along both sides create a physical buffer between sidewalks and moving traffic, reducing random pedestrian-vehicle conflicts mid-block.
Safety is reduced by high mixing: scooters/motorbikes are parked and likely circulate near the curb lane, while cars enter/exit curbside parking, increasing side-swipe and dooring risks.
No marked crosswalks, pedestrian refuge islands, or signalized crossing features are visible in the scene, which can increase crossing risk on a wide, vehicle-dominant roadway.
livability: Active ground-floor storefronts on both sides with continuous frontage (shops under awnings) support daily services and street activity for all users.
Presence of street lighting poles and consistent commercial edges suggests the corridor is intended as a main street with regular access to amenities.
Street looks relatively orderly and clean, and the railings organize pedestrian movement, which can support a more predictable streetscape experience.
sustainability: The corridor appears car-oriented with many parked cars on both sides and multiple general traffic lanes, encouraging private-vehicle use and associated emissions.
There is very limited visible greenery (few/no street trees and little planting), reducing shade, habitat value, and heat-mitigation ecosystem services.
No visible green stormwater features (rain gardens/permeable verges) and extensive impervious asphalt surface suggest limited water-sensitive design.
aesthetics: Buildings on both sides have coherent height and a consistent black-and-white façade style, creating strong visual unity and a recognizable street character.
Traditional-style shop awnings and repeated red lantern elements add cultural/visual interest along the commercial frontage.
The street appears visually organized with consistent railing design and aligned storefronts, though parked vehicles and scooter clutter reduce overall neatness.
comfort: Thermal comfort is likely weak because the street has minimal tree canopy and large asphalt exposure, offering little shade in hot weather.
Physical comfort for walking is reduced by narrow effective sidewalk space due to railings and curbside clutter (dense scooter parking near the shops).
Psychological comfort is mixed: active shops provide passive surveillance, but heavy traffic presence and tight separation space next to parking can feel stressful for pedestrians.
walkability: Continuous storefronts and awnings can encourage walking by providing destinations and some edge protection near shops.
Walkability is constrained by the need to navigate around parked scooters and the apparent lack of generous, unobstructed sidewalk width behind the railings.
Crossing convenience appears limited on this wide street because no crosswalk markings or pedestrian priority features are visible, reducing route connectivity for pedestrians.
bikeability: No dedicated or protected bike lane markings are visible; cyclists would likely need to share space with moving cars and scooters, lowering perceived safety.
Frequent curbside parking increases dooring risk and turning/merging conflicts for anyone cycling along the curb lane.
The roadway feels fast and vehicle-dominant (multiple lanes and long sightlines), which typically discourages cycling for the general population without strong separation.
